assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Melitz model of heterogeneous firms and selection into exporting changed how trade, productivity and welfare gains are analysed. It shifted the unit of analysis from industries to firms and linked trade to aggregate productivity, and it is the base for much quantitative and empirical work. Helpman's contributions with Melitz and Yeaple on exporting versus FDI, and his wider work on trade with increasing returns, add breadth.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central and unambiguous contribution. Helpman has a strong separate record on trade theory and firm-level trade. Redding is a major later contributor, but a two-person prize seems the cleanest attribution.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of confirmation across theory, structural quantification and microdata. The framework is standard in graduate teaching and policy analysis.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would prefer to reward Helpman for his earlier trade and political-economy work rather than the Melitz framework.
Priority and overlap with Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and with Hopenhayn in the industry-dynamics literature.
Trade already received a prize in 2008 (Krugman).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework, with nominal rigidities, microfounded Phillips curves and interest-rate rules, is the workhorse of central-bank practice and of modern macro teaching. Woodford supplied the theoretical synthesis and the welfare-based case for optimal policy, Gali the empirical and analytical development, and Taylor the policy rule and its empirical and policy influence.
assessment.attribution: Highly diffuse. Calvo (staggered pricing), Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans (the medium-scale DSGE model and identification), Smets and Wouters (estimation) and Gertler are all central. Any trio is contestable. I favour Woodford, Gali and Taylor as covering the theory, the framework and the policy rule.
assessment.maturity: Very mature. It has underpinned inflation-targeting practice for decades, though the post-2021 inflation episode renewed debate about the framework's limits.
uncertainties: Three-person limit against a large, overlapping group of contributors.
Perceived tension with the narrative that the framework failed to anticipate the 2008 crisis and the 2021–22 inflation.
Macro-monetary work has been recognised before (Lucas, Sargent and Sims, Kydland and Prescott, Bernanke), so the field may count as relatively saturated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) show how collateral constraints, asset prices and credit amplify and propagate shocks. That is a foundational mechanism in macro-finance and in how financial frictions are modelled in macroeconomics, and it remains central to analysis of crises and credit cycles.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki–Moore is a clear two-person contribution. Gertler and Gilchrist belong to the adjacent financial accelerator and empirical line, and Bernanke already shared the 2022 prize partly for related work. Restricting to the two keeps the attribution clean.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with nearly three decades of influence and strong post-2008 validation.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize (banks and financial crises) may reduce the committee's appetite.
Whether the committee would want Bernanke–Gertler–Gilchrist credited alongside, given the interwoven history.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) turned misallocation into a measurable explanation of cross-country TFP gaps, and the approach is now standard in growth, development and macro-IO. It gave a quantitative reply to the question of why some countries are poor, and it connects to the Restuccia–Rogerson work.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh–Klenow is the core. Restuccia–Rogerson (2008) is an important concurrent and independent contribution, so the choice of two out of three is contestable.
assessment.maturity: More than fifteen years of replication across countries, with both strong extensions and growing debate about measurement.
uncertainties: Disclosed conflict: I have a long-running co-authorship with Peter Klenow. Conflicts are disclosed but not adjudicated here, and the rank should be read with that in mind.
Measurement debates, since measured misallocation can reflect markups, adjustment costs or mismeasurement rather than true distortions.
Attribution between Restuccia–Rogerson and Hsieh–Klenow.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Autor, Levy and Murnane's task framework and the China-shock papers changed understanding of how technology and trade reshape labour demand, polarisation and local labour markets. The research has had a large influence on policy debates and on empirical methods in labour and trade.
assessment.attribution: Autor is the common thread across the task approach and the trade shock. Dorn and Hanson are co-authors of the China shock work. Katz's earlier work on skill-biased demand and Acemoglu's task models are related contributions.
assessment.maturity: Substantial: twenty years for the task framework and a decade or more for the China shock, with ongoing follow-up on persistence and the debate over magnitudes.
uncertainties: Overlap with Acemoglu's recent recognition and with Katz and Goldin's earlier lines of work.
Debate over external validity and long-run effects of the China shock.
Whether the committee would split the technology and trade strands.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Long-run top-income series built from tax data, and later distributional national accounts and wealth estimates, restructured the empirical basis of inequality research and the policy debate. The data infrastructure is a lasting contribution regardless of position on the interpretation.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are central to the top-incomes series, Zucman to wealth and offshore wealth. Atkinson, who is deceased, was a major precursor and cannot be credited, which complicates the narrative.
assessment.maturity: Mature in data terms, and widely replicated and extended. Theoretical interpretations such as r>g remain contested.
uncertainties: Methodological critiques of the wealth and distributional accounts.
Prize-committee caution about policy-advocacy aspects.
The contribution is measurement more than theory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data on intergenerational mobility, with causal estimates of neighbourhood effects, created a new empirical template across public, labour and urban economics. The influence on measurement and policy design is large.
assessment.attribution: Chetty leads, with Hendren central on neighbourhood effects and mobility. Friedman and Katz are important co-authors, and Katz also appears in other contributions.
assessment.maturity: Strong output, though the work is recent and some findings are still being replicated and extended. The prize timing may be early for some strands.
uncertainties: Maturity: recent work, with long-run validation still ongoing.
Chetty's contributions also span other candidates (tax and elasticity work), which complicates field attribution.
Methodological debate on neighbourhood effects and on the stability of the estimates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Double/debiased machine learning and causal-forest-type methods let researchers estimate heterogeneous treatment effects and valid inference with high-dimensional controls. They are a methodological advance used across empirical fields.
assessment.attribution: Chernozhukov (with Chetverikov, Demirer, Duflo, Hansen, Newey and Robins) for DML and Athey (with Imbens and Wager) for causal forests. The collaborative nature and the number of co-authors make the attribution diffuse.
assessment.maturity: Younger than the other candidates, with rapid adoption but a shorter record of confirmation.
uncertainties: Timing: the methods are roughly a decade old.
Attribution among many co-authors, including Newey, Imbens and Robins.
Imbens and Angrist already won in 2021 for related causal-inference methods.
